personalEssay.prompt: Some students have a background, identity, interest, or talent that is so meaningful they believe their application would be incomplete without it. If this sounds like you, then please share your story.
personalEssay.text:
Most people in my school would tell you I'm a wrestler. My mom would tell you I'm a farm kid. I'd tell you those are the same thing.

I live on a farm about eleven miles outside of Le Mars, Iowa, which is the Ice Cream Capital of the World, a fact we are legally required to mention. My family grows corn and soybeans and runs a small cow-calf herd. My great-great-grandpa bought the first eighty acres in 1911. I'm the fifth generation to wake up on this ground, and on most days I'm up before five to feed cattle before school.

Wrestling and farming both start with the same thing, which is doing what you don't want to do before anyone's watching. Nobody sees you check water tanks at 5 a.m. in January when it's nineteen below. Nobody sees you run stairs in a trash bag in the school gym on a Saturday. But you can tell who did it and who didn't. In wrestling, you can tell in the third period. On a farm, you can tell in October.

Junior year I took fifth at state, which is the best anyone from our school has done in a while. I lost my semifinal on a takedown with eleven seconds left, and I was so mad I didn't talk to anybody on the bus ride home from Des Moines. My dad drove separately so he could be at the farm by chores, and when I got home at almost midnight the light was on in the barn. He was in there with a heifer that was having trouble calving. He didn't ask about my match. He just handed me a pair of OB sleeves.

We were out there until two. The calf came backward, which is bad, and for a while it wasn't breathing. My dad cleared its nose and rubbed it with straw and swung it a little by the back legs, and then it coughed and shook its head like it was annoyed with both of us. I remember standing there covered in stuff I won't describe, thinking, okay, I lost a wrestling match. This calf almost lost a lot more than that.

That's not a dramatic lesson, but it's real. Out here, you don't get a lot of time to feel sorry for yourself, because the animals don't care how your day went. That sounds harsh but it's actually kind of freeing. You do the next thing. Then you do the next thing after that.

This season I'm moving up to 160, partly because I grew and partly because I'm done cutting weight in a sauna suit. I want to place higher than I did last year, but honestly I care more about our younger guys. I'm captain now, and I've got three freshmen who remind me exactly of myself, which is to say they think they're tougher than they are. I'm trying to teach them that being tough isn't about not losing. It's about being in the barn at midnight anyway.

I'm also the first person in my family planning to study agriculture at a four-year college instead of just coming home after high school. My dad says he's fine with it as long as I come back with something useful. I want to study agricultural systems management, because the farm of 2040 is going to look a lot different from my grandpa's: more data, more automation, fewer people, more risk. I want to be the one who figures out how to keep a place like ours running.

The heifer calf is a cow now, by the way. She's mean. We named her Fifth Place.

supplements.prompt: How will opportunities at Purdue support your interests, both in and out of the classroom?
supplements.text:
The first time I really thought about Purdue was at the National FFA Convention in Louisville my junior year. There were Purdue students at the career expo showing a planter that adjusted its seeding rate row by row based on soil maps, and I stood there way too long asking questions while the rest of my chapter went to find food. One of the students told me she grew up on a hog farm in Indiana. That was when I realized "precision agriculture" wasn't just something on a seed company's billboard. It was a major, and people like me were doing it.

At Purdue I want to study Agricultural Systems Management in the Department of Agricultural and Biological Engineering. I've fixed enough broken equipment on our farm to know how to keep things running. What I don't know yet is how to design systems that waste less, use data better, and make a 1,200-acre family farm work with fewer people. Purdue's hands-on labs and the chance to do research with faculty who work directly with farmers are exactly what I'm looking for.

Outside of class, I want to join Purdue's Collegiate FFA and keep helping younger kids the way older members helped me. I'd also love to find a club wrestling team, even if I'm not good enough for the Big Ten.

My dad said I can go as long as I come back with something useful. I think Purdue is where I'd find it.
